clue.text: Reveal chap wearing runners on a regular basis

indicators.note: the outer letters wear the chap like a garment, so he goes inside them
every other letter of the word runners is taken, at regular intervals

parts.note: cove is old British slang for a chap or fellow

explanation.surface: Someone unmasks a man jogging alongside athletes at regular intervals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on a regular basis' takes the even letters of runners, U N R, and 'wearing' puts COVE inside them.
explanation.definitionFit: To uncover something is to expose or lay it open, a straightforward synonym for reveal.

clue.text: Drop off university student intercepting a don, surprisingly

indicators.note: the student cuts into the middle of the rearranged letters, intercepting them
surprisingly signals that these letters come out in an unexpected order

parts.note: L is for learner, a student driver's plate

explanation.surface: A university student cuts off a lecturer unexpectedly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surprisingly' turns A DON into NOAD, and 'intercepting' sets L in it after the N.
explanation.definitionFit: To drop off goods or passengers is to unload them from a vehicle.

clue.text: Where one might find fish caught by bohemian

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
a hippy is an unconventional, bohemian type

explanation.surface: Fish caught by a free spirit might end up somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: A CHIPPY is British slang for a fish-and-chip shop.
explanation.definitionFit: A fish-and-chip shop, the chippy in British slang, is the obvious place to buy fish.

clue.text: At heart, loved girl dancing with you so energetically

indicators.note: at heart points to the centre letter of the word loved
dancing letters move about, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A beloved girl dances with her partner with great energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At heart' takes V from loved, and 'dancing' rearranges GIRL YOU SO into IGOROUSLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something vigorously means doing it with force and vitality, so energetically.

clue.text: Mature writer supporting conclusion of younger one

indicators.note: in a down answer the writer sits below the rest, holding it up
the conclusion of the word younger is its final letter

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
a pen is something to write with

explanation.surface: An older writer backs a youngster's ending.
explanation.walkthrough: 'conclusion of' takes R from younger; 'supporting' puts PEN under R and I in this down light.
explanation.definitionFit: To ripen is to grow ready or fully developed, as fruit matures.

clue.text: Sauce — something sailor may use up

parts.note: a ketch is a two-masted sailing boat, which a sailor might use
taken as written

explanation.surface: A condiment, and something a sailor might use up on board.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash invites reading 'something sailor may use up' as one phrase; a ketch is a two-masted sailing boat.
explanation.definitionFit: Ketchup is a familiar tomato condiment poured over chips and burgers, so it is a kind of sauce.

clue.text: King and Harry — we longed for information

parts.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king

indicators.note: to harry is to harass, so these letters are harassed into a new order

explanation.surface: A king and Prince Harry, long sought after for some news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harry' looks like the prince but is the verb harass, rearranging WE LONGED into NOWLEDGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Knowledge is facts and understanding gathered, so it is broadly information.

clue.text: Rubbish, upsetting year for Matt Hancock?

indicators.note: in a down answer upsetting turns the word upside down, so it reads in reverse

parts.note: rot means nonsense or rubbish

explanation.surface: Rubbish, and a distressing year for the politician Matt Hancock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upsetting' turns ROT over into TOR. Matt Hancock is a British Conservative politician, a former health secretary, hence a Tory; the question mark marks him as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Matt Hancock was a Conservative MP and minister, and Tory is the informal name for a Conservative.

clue.text: Funny smell starts to occasionally really overpower us

parts.note: hum is British slang for a bad smell

indicators.note: the starts of these words means their first letters

explanation.surface: A comical stench now and then threatens to overcome us.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starts to' takes O, R, O from the three words; US is taken as written.
explanation.definitionFit: Humorous means amusing or comic, a direct synonym for funny.

clue.text: Papa feels bitter about hosts

parts.note: P is papa in the NATO phonetic alphabet
to resent something is to feel bitter about it

explanation.surface: Dad holds a grudge against the people throwing the party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hosts' is the verb, as a presenter hosts a show.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who presents a television show hosts it, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Creating pork pies from fish with unknown filling

indicators.note: the unknown sits inside the fish like the filling of a pie

parts.note: a ling is a long food fish of the cod family
y is one of the algebraic letters for an unknown quantity

explanation.surface: Someone makes pork pies from fish with a mystery filling.
explanation.walkthrough: PORK PIES is British rhyming slang for lies, so creating them is lying; the surface wants actual meat pies.
explanation.definitionFit: In rhyming slang pork pies are lies, and telling fibs means lying.

clue.text: Plan for golf: hit endlessly

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of
G is golf in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: endlessly means the last letter of the word for hit is dropped

parts.note: rammed means struck or hit hard

explanation.surface: A strategy for a round of golf: just keep hitting the ball.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' cuts the D from RAMMED, leaving RAMME.
explanation.definitionFit: A programme is a planned schedule of events or activities, so it is a plan.

clue.text: Evidently American father perhaps, is immersed in work

indicators.note: the American father is submerged within the word for work

parts.note: to ply a trade is to work at it
a father is one example of a parent

explanation.surface: Apparently, an American dad is lost in his work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'immersed in' signals the enclosure; 'father perhaps' is a definition by example, so the solver must generalise to a parent.
explanation.definitionFit: Evidently and apparently both mean as far as one can see or judge, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Genuine regret after act's conclusion

indicators.note: the word for regret comes after the letter from act's
the conclusion of the word act's is its final letter of the stem, taken here

parts.note: to rue something is to regret it

explanation.surface: Real remorse after a performance has finished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'conclusion' takes T, the last letter of act (the 's goes with it), and RUE follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Something true is real or authentic, just as something genuine is.

clue.text: Having a rabbit making animal noises

definitions.meaning: to rabbit (on) is British slang for to talk at length, so having a rabbit means talking idly
monkeys, birds and squirrels chatter, making rapid noises

explanation.surface: Owning a pet rabbit and making animal sounds.
explanation.walkthrough: RABBIT here is British rhyming slang, rabbit and pork for talk.
explanation.definitionFit: Chattering is both idle gossiping talk and the rapid sounds of monkeys or birds.

clue.text: Reduced rust hadn't affected what fencer might do

parts.note: reduced means cut, as prices are cut

indicators.note: affected means altered, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Corrosion was trimmed back but hadn't changed what a fencer might do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'affected' is the anagram signal; the apostrophe in hadn't is ignored. The phrase now means lively argument, but began in swordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Cut and thrust originally described the slashing and stabbing moves of swordplay, hence of a fencer.

clue.text: Selected a soft tart

parts.note: P is piano, the musical marking for soft
a tart or pointed remark is sharp and cutting

explanation.surface: Someone chose a gentle, sour pastry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tart' is the adjective sharp, not a pastry.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone appointed has been chosen for a role, so selected.

clue.text: Lends adult balls — around 5

parts.note: A is the film certificate abbreviation for adult

indicators.note: the word for balls is around the five, enclosing it

parts.note: balls are formal dances
V is the Roman numeral for five

explanation.surface: Someone loans grown-up sports equipment, around five of them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'balls' are social dances, not sports gear.
explanation.definitionFit: A bank that advances money is lending it, so advances means lends.

clue.text: Deceive badly, admitting new testimony

indicators.note: the rearranged letters admit the new letter, taking it inside
badly signals the letters are put together wrongly, in a new order

explanation.surface: A witness lies poorly while giving fresh testimony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' rearranges DECEIVE into EVIDECE, and 'admitting' lets N in.
explanation.definitionFit: Evidence in court is the testimony and material given, so the two coincide.

clue.text: Events prevent models working without underwear, ultimately

indicators.note: working means being worked over, so the letters are reshaped
without means the extra letter must be left out of the reworked pool
ultimately points to the final letter of the word underwear

explanation.surface: Organisers stop models from walking the catwalk without underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'working' rearranges PREVENT MODELS, and 'without' removes R, the last letter of underwear, as 'ultimately' directs.
explanation.definitionFit: Developments are new happenings or occurrences, so events is a synonym for them.

clue.text: Gaff about Andrew's first royal residence

indicators.note: the home goes about the letter, surrounding it

parts.note: gaff is British slang for a home, or one's place

indicators.note: first means the opening letter of the word Andrew's

explanation.surface: A gaffe involving Prince Andrew at a royal home.
explanation.walkthrough: GAFF is British slang for a house; 'about' puts PLACE around A, the first of Andrew's.
explanation.definitionFit: A palace is the official home of a monarch, the grandest royal residence.

clue.text: Pressure from headmistress? Not half!

indicators.note: not half means only one half of the word headmistress is kept, here the back half

explanation.surface: Is a headmistress under pressure? Absolutely!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' is British slang for very much so, but here it drops the front half, HEADMI.
explanation.definitionFit: Stress is mental or physical strain, which is a kind of pressure.

clue.text: Helps servants to remove male

indicators.note: to remove means the male letter is taken out of the servants

parts.note: maids are female household servants

explanation.surface: Domestic staff assist in getting rid of a man.
explanation.definitionFit: Aids as a verb means assists or supports, the same as helps.

clue.text: Officer lenient but a criminal scratches bishop

indicators.note: criminal suggests the letters are crooked, so they are rearranged
scratches means removes, as a horse is scratched from a race

parts.note: B is the chess notation abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A judge is lenient, but a crook strikes off a cleric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'criminal' rearranges LENIENT BUT A, and 'scratches' removes the B for bishop.
explanation.definitionFit: A lieutenant is a junior commissioned rank in the army or navy, so is an officer.

clue.text: Part of lower steering mechanism on boat with no top

indicators.note: in a down answer the top is the first letter, which is removed

parts.note: a rudder is the blade that steers a boat

explanation.surface: A component of a low-slung steering device on a topless boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lower' is a cow, which lows; the surface wants the comparative of low.
explanation.definitionFit: An udder is the milk gland of a cow, and a cow is something that lows.

clue.text: Drink some sip in tavern

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Have a little sip of something in the pub.
explanation.definitionFit: A pint of beer is the standard serving ordered in a pub, so a drink.

clue.text: Given time, prisoner struggled outside court

parts.note: con is short for convict, a prisoner

indicators.note: the word for struggled goes outside the court, enclosing it

parts.note: vied means competed or struggled

explanation.surface: A sentenced inmate fought on outside the courtroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Given time' is slang for being sentenced to prison.
explanation.definitionFit: To be given time is to receive a prison sentence, which follows being found guilty.

clue.text: Picture that is in magazine? The opposite!

indicators.note: in would put the first piece inside the second
the opposite says to swap the roles, so the magazine goes inside instead

parts.note: i.e. abbreviates id est, that is

explanation.surface: Is that a picture found in a magazine? No, quite the reverse!
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' read literally gives the wrong nesting; 'The opposite!' tells the solver to swap container and contents.
explanation.definitionFit: An image is a visual representation such as a photograph, so it is a picture.

clue.text: Small coin Edward picked up

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a cent is a small coin
Ed is the short form of the name Edward

explanation.surface: Edward bent down and picked up a tiny coin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'picked up' means detected by smell, not lifted.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog that scented a trail has picked up its smell, so the two mean detected.

clue.text: Feels sorry for river birds

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for river on maps
egrets are white wading birds of the heron family

explanation.surface: Someone pities the birds of the river.
explanation.definitionFit: To regret something is to feel sorrow or remorse about it.
